title: The season word
hook: every haiku holds a season word, placing it in the year

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: what I have seen. Tagore's goodbye was a thank-you to the world. Today, a new country and a new kind of poem: Japan, and the haiku, where one small word does the work of a whole season.
screen: `WHAT I HAVE SEEN.` → `JAPAN, AND THE HAIKU.`

segments.voice: A smell can tell you the month before your calendar does: cut grass, wood smoke, the first cold air at the bus stop. Japanese poets built that into the form. A traditional haiku carries a kigo, a season word: a frog for spring, cicadas for summer, the autumn wind, a withered field for winter. Say the word, and the whole season walks in with it, without the poem ever naming the month.
screen: `A SMELL BEFORE THE CALENDAR.` → `KIGO: THE SEASON WORD.` → `THE WHOLE SEASON WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: Here's one by Matsuo Basho, the poet this path will walk with for a few days. In Japanese: furuike ya, kawazu tobikomu, mizu no oto. An old pond. A frog jumps in. The sound of water. The frog is the season word. It's spring, and the poem never says so. Poets even keep almanacs of season words, called saijiki, sorted by the time of year, so a few syllables can carry the weight of the whole year. That's the craft. Here's the teaching underneath it. Basho's student Doho wrote down something the master told his students: learn about the pine from the pine, and about bamboo from bamboo. Don't force your own ideas onto a thing. Go into it, and wait until its own life shows. Basho had studied Zen with a priest named Butcho, and readers find two marks of that Buddhist training in his poems: close attention to exactly this moment, and the knowledge that this moment is passing. A season word does both at once. It pins the poem to now: this frog, this pond, this spring. And in the same breath it reminds you that spring will end. In this tradition you don't escape time to find what's real. You notice, very closely, which season it is, and what's real is already there, splashing.
screen: `AN OLD POND. A FROG JUMPS IN.` · `SAIJIKI: AN ALMANAC OF SEASONS.` · `LEARN THE PINE FROM THE PINE.` · `THIS MOMENT, AND IT'S PASSING.` · then, large: `THE SEASON WORD.`

segments.voice: Step outside or open a window, and use your senses to find today's season word: one smell, sound or sight that could only belong to this time of year. Don't decorate it; let it be exactly what it is. When you've found it, say it once, quietly, like the first line of a haiku.
Kigo: the season word in a haiku. One concrete image, a frog, a cicada, a withered field, that places the poem in the turning year.
Your line: the season word. One small image, and the whole year turns behind it. Talk tomorrow.
